items.readable_text:
Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
when the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has at least one zero eigenvalue.

Content:
A zero eigenvalue is special because [MATH: e^{0\cdot t}=1,] so the corresponding component of a solution has no exponential growth or decay. Geometrically, this often creates a line of equilibrium points (infinitely many fixed points), instead of a single equilibrium at the origin.

Content:
Indeed, equilibrium points satisfy [MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\mathbf{0},] so for [MATH: \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}] we solve
[MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]
That is, equilibrium points form the null space of [MATH: A.]

Content:
- If [MATH: \det(A) \neq 0,] then the null space is [MATH: \{\mathbf{0}\}] and the only equilibrium is the origin.
- If [MATH: \det(A)=0,] then the null space contains infinitely many points (typically a line through the origin in [MATH: 2\times2] cases).

Content:
A zero eigenvalue guarantees [MATH: \det(A)=0], so in that case the null space is nontrivial.

Content:
Let's see a concrete example.

items.title: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

key_prerequisites.name: Solving 2x2 Singular Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

sections.normalized_html: [MATH: {x^{′}(t) = 2x(t) + 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = 5x(t) + 5y(t)] Find an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above.
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = 2x(t) + 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = 5x(t) + 5y(t)]
Find an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have [MATH: [2|2; 5|5]] where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system [MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)] are the points for which [MATH: \mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.] So, we get the following system of linear equations: [MATH: {2x + 2y = 0; 5x + 5y = 0]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get [MATH: 2x+2y=0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad 2y=-2x \quad\Rightarrow\quad y=-x.]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

This determines the line with the equation [MATH: y=-x.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=0] and [MATH: \lambda_2\neq 0] with eigenvectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
Then, the eigenvector direction for [MATH: \lambda_1=0] gives a line of equilibria:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_E = c_1 \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad c_1 \in \mathbb{R}]

Content:
The other eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2] determines what happens off the equilibrium line:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] trajectories move away from the equilibrium line (unstable direction).
- If [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] trajectories move toward the equilibrium line (stable direction).

Content:
A typical solution has the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2,
\qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
So trajectories are parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2,] shifted by the equilibrium vector [MATH: c_1\mathbf{v}_1.]

Content:
To illustrate, let's consider the following example
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x(t) − 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = − x(t) + 2y(t)]
where we know the eigenvalues of the system's matrix are [MATH: \lambda_1=0] and [MATH: \lambda_2=3,] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: [2; 1]] and [MATH: [− 1; 1]] respectively.

Content:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Content:
The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

Content:
- First, notice that [MATH: [2; 1]] are the equilibrium solutions of the system since [MATH: \mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.] These solutions form the line with the equation [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x] in the phase space, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d9a0cb6aea063e7d938b9218221c580a]

Content:
- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to [MATH: [− 1; 1]] has the equation
[MATH: y= -x]
and the straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [− 1; 1]]
lie on that line. Since [MATH: e^{3t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions approach infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/797029119444de0f10795c0a00694204]

Content:
All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.] So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

Graphic:

Now, suppose a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system has a repeated zero eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda=0] (multiplicity [MATH: 2]). Here, the vector field carries no exponential growth or decay in any direction.
There are two subcases.

• If there are two independent eigenvectors (we have a zero matrix), then every direction behaves like an equilibrium direction, and solutions are constant: [MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=\mathbf{x}(0).] So every point is an equilibrium, and the phase portrait is a field of zero vectors.

    • [MATH: \mathbf{x}_E=c_1\mathbf{v}] still gives a line of equilibrium points, while

    • other trajectories align with the eigenspace structure, yielding a shear flow where solutions grow linearly with [MATH: t] (algebraic growth).

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this topic, we'll study phase portraits of linear systems
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]
when the [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A] has at least one zero eigenvalue.

Content:
A zero eigenvalue is special because [MATH: e^{0\cdot t}=1,] so the corresponding component of a solution has no exponential growth or decay. Geometrically, this often creates a line of equilibrium points (infinitely many fixed points), instead of a single equilibrium at the origin.

Content:
Indeed, equilibrium points satisfy [MATH: \mathbf{x}'=\mathbf{0},] so for [MATH: \mathbf{x}'=A\mathbf{x}] we solve
[MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]
That is, equilibrium points form the null space of [MATH: A.]

Content:
- If [MATH: \det(A) \neq 0,] then the null space is [MATH: \{\mathbf{0}\}] and the only equilibrium is the origin.
- If [MATH: \det(A)=0,] then the null space contains infinitely many points (typically a line through the origin in [MATH: 2\times2] cases).

Content:
A zero eigenvalue guarantees [MATH: \det(A)=0], so in that case the null space is nontrivial.

Content:
Let's see a concrete example.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding Equilibrium Points of a System

Example Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = 2x(t) + 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = 5x(t) + 5y(t)]
Find an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
[MATH: [2|2; 5|5]]
where [MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system [MATH: \mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)] are the points for which [MATH: \mathbf{f}(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.] So, we get the following system of linear equations:
[MATH: {2x + 2y = 0; 5x + 5y = 0]

Notice that the second equation is a multiple of the first one. So, we can disregard the second equation.

From the first equation, we get
[MATH: 2x+2y=0
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
2y=-2x
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
y=-x.]

Therefore, the equilibrium points are given by
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

This determines the line with the equation [MATH: y=-x.]

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x(t) + y(t); y^{′}(t) = 2x(t) + 2y(t)]
Which of the following gives all equilibrium points of the system of linear differential equations above?

Choices:
a. [MATH: [x(t); y(t)] = [1; 2]] only
b. [MATH: [x(t); y(t)] = [k; k], k ∈ R]
c. [MATH: [x(t); y(t)] = [0; 0]] only
d. [MATH: [x(t); y(t)] = [k; 2k], k ∈ R]
e. [MATH: [x(t); y(t)] = [k; − k], k ∈ R]

---

Item 4 — Question 2

Prompt:
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x(t) + y(t); y^{′}(t) = x(t) + y(t)]
Which of the following gives an equation of the line in the phase space that contains all equilibrium points of the system above?

Choices:
a. [MATH: y = − x]
b. [MATH: y = x]
c. [MATH: y = − x − 1]
d. [MATH: y = 2x]
e. [MATH: y = − 2x]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Systems With One Zero Eigenvalue

Content:
Suppose a [MATH: 2 \times 2] system has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=0] and [MATH: \lambda_2\neq 0] with eigenvectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
Then, the eigenvector direction for [MATH: \lambda_1=0] gives a line of equilibria:
[MATH: \mathbf{x}_E = c_1 \mathbf{v}_1, \qquad c_1 \in \mathbb{R}]

Content:
The other eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2] determines what happens off the equilibrium line:

Content:
- If [MATH: \lambda_2>0,] trajectories move away from the equilibrium line (unstable direction).
- If [MATH: \lambda_2<0,] trajectories move toward the equilibrium line (stable direction).

Content:
A typical solution has the form
[MATH: \mathbf{x}(t)=c_1\mathbf{v}_1 + c_2 e^{\lambda_2 t}\mathbf{v}_2,
\qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}.]

Content:
So trajectories are parallel to [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2,] shifted by the equilibrium vector [MATH: c_1\mathbf{v}_1.]

Content:
To illustrate, let's consider the following example
[MATH: {x^{′}(t) = x(t) − 2y(t); y^{′}(t) = − x(t) + 2y(t)]
where we know the eigenvalues of the system's matrix are [MATH: \lambda_1=0] and [MATH: \lambda_2=3,] with corresponding eigenvectors [MATH: [2; 1]] and [MATH: [− 1; 1]] respectively.

Content:
Let's sketch the phase portrait of the system.

Content:
The general solution of the system is
[MATH: [x(t); y(t)]]

Content:
- First, notice that [MATH: [2; 1]] are the equilibrium solutions of the system since [MATH: \mathbf{x}'_E(t) = \mathbf{0}.] These solutions form the line with the equation [MATH: y=\dfrac{1}{2}x] in the phase space, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d9a0cb6aea063e7d938b9218221c580a]

Content:
- Now, the line that passes through the origin and is parallel to [MATH: [− 1; 1]] has the equation
[MATH: y= -x]
and the straight-line solutions of the form
[MATH: [− 1; 1]]
lie on that line. Since [MATH: e^{3t} \to \infty] as [MATH: t \to \infty,] these solutions approach infinity as [MATH: t \to \infty.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/797029119444de0f10795c0a00694204]

Content:
All other non-equilibrium solutions are parallel to the vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.] So, the phase portrait of our system looks as follows:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f8bc061c5ebd1d33bfc1892a1daad387]

---
